did_you_know.text: The words “statutes” and “laws” describe two kinds of commandments: statutes are established rules, while laws often concern justice between people.
The warning not to add to or subtract from the commandments emphasizes following the Torah faithfully rather than changing it for personal convenience.
Baal-peor was a deity worshiped in the region of Moab, and the story connected with it appears at length in Numbers, chapter 25.
The verse presents memory as a family responsibility: people must not only remember for themselves, but also teach their children and grandchildren.
Horeb is another biblical name for Mount Sinai, so both names refer to the revelation of the Torah in the wilderness.
Many ancient religions represented their gods with statues, but this passage emphasizes hearing a voice without seeing any figure or image.
“The Ten Words” is the biblical name for the Ten Commandments; they are described as being written on two stone tablets.
The sun, moon, and stars were objects of worship in many ancient cultures, especially in Egypt and Mesopotamia.
“The iron furnace” is a metaphor for the harsh conditions of slavery in Egypt, not a claim that the people literally lived inside a furnace.
The word “venoshantem” is related to the root meaning “old” or “settled,” describing a people established in the land for many generations.
Calling heaven and earth as witnesses resembles the language of a court or covenant, where witnesses are summoned to confirm what was said.
The verb “you will seek” can describe a serious search or appeal; the verse stresses that seeking God requires one’s whole heart and soul.
The cities of refuge were legal institutions intended to protect someone who had killed accidentally while the circumstances were being examined.
The verse distinguishes accidental killing from murder motivated by prior hatred—a distinction that remains important in modern legal systems.
The three cities of refuge east of the Jordan were located within the territories of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh.
Mount Hermon is one of the highest mountains in the Levant, and its snow helps supply springs and streams in the surrounding region.
